comments.author: Erman Taylan
comments.comment: The “own the harness, not the model” point is the one I’d watch closest. For most teams, the durable moat is the eval set, tool contract, retrieval layer, rollback path, and feedback loop, because the frontier model underneath will keep changing every few months.

comments.author: Nav 𓅯 Rao
comments.comment:
Less turns is useful, but I’d track “avoidable turns” separately from total turns.

A harness can look better by forcing early commits, while silently increasing rework later. The metric I’d want is cost per accepted patch after tests, formatting, and reviewer-style checks pass.

comments.author: Aviram Fireberger
comments.comment: Persistent agents become useful when they stop being “smart chat” and start owning boring state: preferences, recurring constraints, pending decisions, and stale reminders. The hard part is evals - checking whether memory retrieval actually improves outcomes instead of just making the agent sound more personal.

comments.author: Zahra Bahrololoumi CBE
comments.comment:
A useful test for “hands off” is whether the agent can recover from partial failure without making the blast radius bigger.

In production, autonomy is less about giving the model more tools and more about tightening the loop around permissions, observability, evals, rollback, and human escalation. The hard part is knowing which decisions should stay reversible, and which should never be delegated without review.
